DunHero: Roguelike RPG, developed and published by Dev Kacper, delivers a compelling blend of action, role-playing, and roguelike elements that has resonated well within the indie gaming community. From the moment you start, it’s clear that this game aims to strike a balance between challenge and accessibility, with a pixel art aesthetic that’s charming yet functional. The gameplay centers around selecting from a diverse cast of nine unique characters, each bringing their own abilities and starting gear to the table, which immediately encourages experimentation and a variety of playstyles. This choice sets the tone for a game designed with replayability in mind, as no two characters feel quite the same and each run offers a fresh strategic experience. The combat system in DunHero is straightforward but demands skill and adaptability. Enemies are varied, with distinct behaviors that force the player to constantly adjust their tactics. The procedurally generated worlds further enhance this challenge, making each run feel unpredictable and exciting. Players explore dungeons populated not only with foes but also with NPCs, traders, and rare elite enemies, creating moments of tension and reward. The randomization of levels and encounters adds a layer of freshness to the game that prevents it from becoming repetitive, while still maintaining a cohesive experience that feels fair despite its difficulty. One of DunHero’s standout features is its extensive itemization system. With over 200 items ranging from weapons and armor to powerful cards and artifacts, players have the freedom to craft builds tailored to their preferred playstyle. The inclusion of item sets that provide bonuses when equipped together introduces a satisfying strategic layer, encouraging players to hunt for specific combinations and synergies. This depth in customization is a highlight, as it offers meaningful choices that can drastically alter the way a run unfolds, whether you opt for raw damage, survivability, or utility. It’s clear that a lot of thought went into balancing these items to ensure variety without overwhelming players. Progression in DunHero is also designed to keep players engaged over the long term. Beyond the immediate challenge of surviving a single run, the game features a meta-progression system where players earn rewards that carry over between sessions. This system not only adds a sense of accomplishment but also unlocks new characters and difficulty modes, providing motivation to continue pushing forward. Such progression helps to mitigate the roguelike’s inherent difficulty spikes by offering tangible growth that persists beyond the death of a single hero, making subsequent runs feel increasingly rewarding. Multiplayer functionality allows up to four players to join forces, adding a social dimension that can transform the experience entirely. Playing cooperatively introduces new dynamics, as team coordination becomes essential to overcoming tougher enemies and bosses. While this feature adds significant value, there have been some reports of technical issues, including lag and occasional bugs, especially when playing on less powerful hardware like the Steam Deck. These issues can detract from the experience but don’t overshadow the core gameplay’s strengths. Visually, DunHero embraces a pixel art style that, while not flashy, suits its gameplay perfectly. The art is clear enough to communicate important information during fast-paced combat and exploration, and the environments are diverse enough to keep players visually interested. Complementing this aesthetic is a well-crafted soundtrack composed by Miguel Angell, which helps to set the mood whether you’re cautiously navigating a dungeon or engaged in a frantic battle. The audio design, although understated, does an admirable job of enhancing immersion without overpowering the gameplay. Despite its many strengths, DunHero is not without flaws. Some players have pointed out that the difficulty curve can sometimes feel uneven, with certain enemy patterns or boss encounters feeling unfair or overly punishing. This can occasionally lead to frustration, particularly for newcomers to the roguelike genre. Additionally, while the game offers a wealth of items and characters, the narrative elements are relatively sparse, which might leave those looking for a deep story or character development wanting more. The focus here is very much on gameplay mechanics and challenge rather than storytelling. Overall, DunHero: Roguelike RPG stands as a robust and enjoyable addition to the roguelike genre. Its blend of strategic combat, extensive customization options, and procedural variety makes for a game that is both engaging and challenging. While there are areas that could benefit from polishing—particularly in balancing difficulty and expanding narrative content—the game’s active development and passionate community indicate a promising future. For players who enjoy a demanding roguelike experience with plenty of room for strategic depth and replayability, DunHero is definitely worth exploring. Rating: 8/10

28个可玩职业！大量的各具特色的武器！可雇佣村民，可杀人越货！ 地牢发现！地牢探险！BOSS击杀！ 小极品！！游戏的深度需要多次进入才能逐渐了解，肉鸽机制下藏了不少东西，绝不是随便进去看两眼就能明白游戏体验的。 另外，这个游戏有人说抄袭小小肉鸽，其实是过于言过其实的话， 看看战斗场景和小小肉鸽很像吗？ 这个地图怎么设计的，跟铁锤守卫很像，地图上有一些可拾取的资源，也有一堆堆扎堆的怪物，装备可以刷落，也会刷出精英怪 但这个游戏你可以在地图上雇佣NPC， 可以去夺取NPC的箱子，可以击杀整个屋子的NPC（前提要记得先把想买的东西买好） 地图还有需要钥匙开启的宝箱，可变成宝箱怪的宝箱，还可以需要炸弹炸开的隐藏地牢入口/竞技场入口，和BOSS房。 这些能跟小小肉鸽是一回事吗？ 这游戏很容易让人觉得容易联想到小小肉鸽的就是有很多可玩职业，但那也不是小小肉鸽独家设计。 至于说可以捡武器（武器相当多），随时换武器，那不是所有ARPG基本的特征吗？ 而且它的升级卡牌基本都是基础数据，并不会产生什么技能型的构筑影响。 单纯就是肉鸽的临场属性提升。 我相信随着玩下去会看到越来越多的深化的内容。 游戏总有雷同的地方，但差异化处理的部分才是游戏真正的核心特征。

Score: 2/5 Maybe recommendable for bullet hell veterans, which I am not. [b]The Good[/b] Visuals are simple, but colorful and everything was distinct. Audio is fine. Decent number of classes, although they were not impactful on how I played the game. Some of the upgrades/gear felt good to use or presenting interesting choices. Some variation in enemy attack patterns. [b]The Bad[/b] Difficulty/challenge is achieved by throwing insane numbers of enemies who can infinitely summon reinforcements and very restricted healing options. Extreme difficulty spike on second level. Never made it past beginning of second level. All enemies and weapons fire projectiles, including melee ones. Gameplay gets stale in under an hour. Difficult to not hit allies in a brawl, which is most of the time. So decide between accidently becoming a murderer with consequences, or using allies as fodder while standing back or very carefully getting in pot shots at enemies until all your allies die.

Game is a lot of fun for few dollars. Highly recommended if you are looking for something akin to Tiny Rogues or Streets of Rogue. It takes best concepts out of those two titles, with better or worse result, and blends them into one coherent bundle. I have only few gripes with this game. Namely: - Items and item sets are like 75% times taken from Tiny Rogues with little alterations to facilitate them into different game model. I get that developers were inspired by that title, but holly molly. - Balance is not there. It's either you die in two first levels or transcend into godhood and steamroll till end. Challenges just kinda pad this out, but they only prolong the steamroll part for like 1-2 stages. - Some achievements and character unlocks are straight up bugged. Two big outliers are true hero and ninja. I got the requirements for both few times, but none triggered properly. (For those who read this and want to unlock true hero, use true hero sword from the hotbar to equip it. Equiping it from blacksmith does not trigger unlock. Sadly I don't have walkaround for ninja tho) Overall 7/10. Great to kill some time on a Sunday with friends

I was NOT expecting to have so much fun with this little game! I got it as a gift from a friend at work, and didn't really think much of it. In fact, I thought I'd end up just playing it for like an hour or two and get bored. Instead what I ended up finding was a hidden gem that really deserves more recognition for its really fun roguelike gameplay loop! Outside of like 2 hours I played this exclusively on the Steam Deck and it ended up being perfect for that format, especially if you're looking for something casual in bed. DunHero scratched the itch I had after Hades, a game I found myself playing a session or two every night before going to sleep. I had been looking for something quick, unique with each run, and fun since Hades. This game ended up fitting the bill pretty close. There are several mechanics that make each run unique and fun to play, providing a great roguelike experience: [list] [*]There are a plethora of "heroes" to chose from, all unique from one another. They have different points in the main three stats: strength, dex, and magic. Additionally, they start off with weapons unique to who they are and carry perks that are specific to them. As a base, this provides a lot of early flexibility in strategy for how you want to play a run. Maybe you want to stack poison on enemies, or specialize in burning, or heck, even make smithing your weapons more potent! The game provides that from that get go and it helps with making each run unique. [*]There are base progression perks that make runs "easier" over time. These are attained by, well, doing more runs! Over time you'll gain points to put into different perks as you see fit. It's a nice incentive to make you play the game, feeding back into the gameplay loop. [*]No one run is the same. The dungeons, loot/weapons, perks, enemies, allied villages, etc. are all randomized with each one. This is what REALLY made DunHero addictive for me. Every time I'd finish a run, I'd think "okay let's try one more time, and see what strat I came make this go." [/list] [b] I do have some critical feedback on the game though incase the developer is reading this. These are bugs mainly for Steam Deck play: [/b] [list] [*]The Steam Deck's controls aren't properly linked to menus in the game. Sometimes I have to use the touchscreen to re-enable highlighting a for D-pad/joystick navigation of menus. The most egregious case of this is when I beat the game and the final text with the "Play Again" button comes up. Not matter what I do, I can't get the button to highlight and click it; I'm stuck on that screen. Every time I reach the end of a run and come upon this, I have to force quit out the game and re-open it. [*]I don't know if this is a bug... But sometimes in the menu of a trader, when pressing A to chose "Trade" I get magically teleported to a different location (usually another house or the level boss entrance). I think this may be happening when no option is highlighted to chose when in the menu (going back to the previous bug described). [*]On Steam Deck, I think the buttons are mapped to PlayStation Icons. Not a major thing, but I had to mentally remember what button needed pressing whenever the square icon came up for example. I can't remember if this was also the case for controllers on my time on PC. [/list] I hope these can get fixed, but outside of that feedback I had a wonderful time with this game and will be recommending it to others.

Sometimes a game manages to distill a genre down to the simple components that make it fun, and that was DunHero for me. This game actually started me off on my twin-stick shooter/bullet heaven kick. Does it do anything groundbbreaking? Nope. Is it fun? Hell yeah. It just does what it does well. One thing that is on the more unique side is that DunHero doesn’t use discreet rooms; each level is an open map with topography that produces vague room-like areas but that you can explore however you want. I really liked this, and I wish more games in this genre did that. In addition to giving it an exploration vibe, it also meant you could figure out how to approach mobs instead of them just being auto-aggro’d when you enter a room. I definitely had runs where I had a crappy build that I pushed through by strafing enemies and hitting them through walls with auras. I like when games give you the choice to do stupid things like that. I liked the variety of classes, but it did have the issue of like, here are your starting classes and you can use them to unlock the better versions. There wasn’t really much of a reason to go back to a class once you’d gotten the “better” one; I would have enjoyed some kind of reward, even like, a statue in town, for clearing a class, and then something big for getting a win with everyone. Mostly I wanted an excuse to keep going after seeing everything, lol. I also really enjoyed Hell Mode. The original game was medium-ish difficulty, the heat modifiers were nice, but trying to clear Hell Mode was a real challenge and I had a lot of fun slowly figuring out the best approach and then finally getting there.

The solo Developer that made DunHero should be very pleased with themselves. This game is excellent and although there are definitely bugs, this was a wild ride. I am going to hang about and collect the rest of the character classes, but I have enjoyed every minute spent playing DunHero. There are 31 classes presently in game and each of them offer a different experience. I greatly enjoyed the roguelite upgrades throughout each run. Each playthrough is effectively like a campaign in a dungeon crawler and that's really impressive. There are loads of different weapons to use and a wealth of equipment to build up powerful effects within builds. The combat isn't groundbreaking, but is well refined in its simplicity. This is one I'm going to throw my kids at when they're ready. If there were some more depth to the endgame; synergies, items that extend reach or change the way weapon attacks behave, this would be the best game I've played all year in this genre. I'm eager to try whatever this dev has to offer though. If you're into this genre, don't walk, run. This is worth your time.
